Mat & Vic's

Synthesis of performance for Stefan and Nadja

June 29, 2026

I went through the whole account, and the short version is that the setup is fine. The 30 cotton ads are live, in the right campaign, pointed at the right page. The cost cap is set a touch tight, which is keeping delivery low, and that's a quick thing to loosen. So there's no glitch to hunt down here. The reason the ads aren't getting traction sits a layer underneath the account, and I think it's worth walking through properly rather than just nudging a setting.

The way I see it, you've got two paths from here. One keeps the setup roughly as it is and just changes how the media gets bought. It's quick, you could start today, and in my read it has under a 10% chance of getting the Shopify side to the €15,000 a month you set as your Q1 goal back in January, which is €180,000 for the year. The other path means changing a few things that are harder to change, and it's the less comfortable one because it's real work instead of a switch you flip. Done properly though, I'd put it around 90% to get you there. I'd rather lay both out plainly than pretend the easy one is more than it is.

Path 1

Keep the setup, adjust the media buying

<10% to your goal

This path is mostly about the media buying. There are two moves here, and you can run them together. They're different in how much I'd lean on them, so I'll say where I stand on each as we go. One of them I'd genuinely set up, and the other I'd only run to scratch an itch. Since Nadja's already in Claude Code, I've written each one as a prompt you can paste straight in.

1. A plain auto-bid campaign. This is the one I wouldn't run myself. No cost cap and no ROAS goal, just normal auto-bidding on Highest Volume, with every ad we've made in one campaign. The idea is that Meta sometimes needs a spark of spend to get moving. I'd put low odds on it changing much, and I've run it enough times to feel comfortable saying that. But plenty of people who came up on auto-bidding like seeing spend come through, and some things you just have to feel out yourself before you trust they're a dead end. So I'd only do this one if you've got that itch to scratch.

The budget matters more here than you'd think. I'd set it to about €225 a day, which is five times your CPA. It has to be that high because Meta needs roughly 50 conversions a week to get an ad set out of the learning phase and settle down, and at a €45 CPA that takes real spend to reach. Starve the budget and it never gathers enough conversions to learn, so it stays stuck and the numbers bounce around without ever stabilising. So go in expecting this first stretch to be you paying for Meta to learn, not to turn a clean profit. You're buying stable data, and you read it once it's had enough volume to mean something.
Prompt to paste into Claude Code:
In our Mat & Vic's Meta ad account, set up one new auto-bid campaign.

- Objective: Sales (conversions), optimising for the Purchase event on our pixel.
- Bid strategy: Highest Volume. Do NOT set a cost cap and do NOT set a ROAS goal.
- One ad set, broad targeting (Germany + Austria), and put every cotton ad we already
  built into it (the Baumwoll-Ratgeber batch).
- Daily budget: 225 EUR.
- Leave it paused at the end so I can review before it goes live.

Before you make changes, fetch the current live Meta Marketing API docs so you are
working off today's parameters, not stale training data. Then confirm exactly what you
created.
2. Your current campaign, duplicated as a ROAS-goal campaign. This one I'd actually set up. It keeps everything you've already got and just swaps the bid strategy, so there's nothing to rebuild, and a ROAS goal tells Meta to aim for a return that's tied to your economics instead of a flat cost per sale. Set the goal at 2.5 to start, which is conservative. On its own it won't fix what's throttling your scale, but of the two moves on this path it's the one I'd genuinely run, and you can leave the auto-bid one for if you want to scratch that itch too.
Prompt to paste into Claude Code:
In our Mat & Vic's Meta ad account, duplicate our current cost-cap campaign in full.

- Copy the entire campaign: every ad set, and every ad inside each ad set.
- Change the new campaign's bid strategy from Cost Cap to ROAS goal.
- Set the ROAS goal at the AD-SET level (not the campaign level) to 2.5.
- Keep the same budgets and targeting as the original.
- Leave it paused at the end so I can review before it goes live.

Before you make changes, fetch the current live Meta Marketing API docs so you are
working off today's parameters, not stale training data. Then confirm exactly what you
created.

So I'd put the ROAS-goal one in, and run the auto-bid alongside it only if you want to feel that one out. Either way, neither of them is what changes your trajectory, because the thing actually holding you back sits underneath all of this, and that's the next path.

Path 2

Fix the foundation: your unit economics

~90% to your goal

Your Cotton Classic 10-pack is €49.99, which works out to $5.70 a pair. The bundles come down to around $3 a pair. I've been shopping for socks myself this past week so this is fresh for me, and that price is going to be hard to grow on. At $5.70 a pair you're priced right where Uniqlo is, and Uniqlo can sell socks that cheap because they're enormous and they make their money across a whole store. A small brand selling mostly socks doesn't have that to lean on.

Hollow Socks is the one I'd point to. Same category as you, but their socks run $17 to $35 a pair even in the bundles, and they're an eight-figure brand. That's not because alpaca is magic. It's because they were deliberate about their unit economics from the start, and the margin that gives them is what lets them stay competitive and profitable at the same time. Right now you're short on both, and the reason traces back to selling at roughly 50% margin.

That's the part I want you to sit with. When you're working off a 50% margin, it's like playing a video game with one hand on the controller. You can still play, you just can't beat the people using both hands. And everything we'd do together on the ads and the funnels sits downstream of that number, so we could keep making the creative sharper forever and it still won't fix a margin that's too thin to pay for the next customer.

Here's the bind you're in right now. At your current price you're not competitive enough in the auction, so Meta throttles your delivery, which is the exact thing you've been seeing. And even when a sale does come through, the margin is too thin to actually profit. You're caught below the spot where both of those work.

So the work I'd start with isn't the ads. It's getting your gross margin up toward 70 or 80%, which means pricing closer to where a premium brand prices. The cleanest way to do that is a proper bundle ladder, the same idea Hollow uses, where the per-pair price is high but bigger packs feel like a better deal.

Here's what that could look like for you, using the cost figures you shared with us in January.

PackPrice$ / pairGross marginAllowable CPA (BE to 20%)
6 pairs€79$15.0267%€37 to €53
12 pairs€129$12.2669%€63 to €89
18 pairs€169$10.7170%€84 to €118
24 pairs€199$9.4669%€98 to €138

A ladder like this puts you at 67 to 70% margin, and it lets you pay anywhere from €37 to €118 for a sale depending on the pack, instead of the €13 you can afford today.

To see why that range matters so much, here's what raising the price does to the one number you live and die by in the auction, which is the most you can afford to pay for a sale.

It's the same business and the same socks. At $5 a pair today you can pay about €13 for a sale and keep 20%. At $10 a pair you could pay €40 for that same margin, which is three times the room to compete for a customer. That's a different game than scraping for the cheapest possible click.

Now I know there's a real wrinkle here, which is Amazon. What you sell on Amazon limits what you can do on the Shopify store, since the pricing has to line up across the two. So I'm not suggesting you just raise the price on the exact products you're running on Amazon. What I think you'll eventually need to do is take these same socks and put them out as their own products on the DTC side, under different names and SKUs, maybe with a small tweak to the product itself, so they can stand on their own and carry premium pricing. It's more work up front. But without the margin to sustain it, the Shopify side stays a hard game, and it's a hard game to keep playing once you've seen how it goes. I've been in it before.

The reason I keep coming back to the margin is that it's the actual bottleneck. You can spend weeks tuning the campaign type and the bidding, which is everything in Path 1, but if the margin is the narrow point, none of that tuning changes how much gets through.

The play

How I'd run it from here

For the media buying, I'd put in the ROAS-goal campaign from Path 1 and let it run, since that's the one of the two that's actually worth setting up. And if you've got the itch to rule out a bug or just watch some spend move, run the auto-bid test alongside it. I don't expect that one to change much, but some things you have to taste for yourself before you believe them, the way I can describe vanilla ice cream to you all day and you still won't really know it until you've had a spoonful. So turn that stone over, see there's nothing under it, and move on.

The two things I'd actually keep running are these. The first is building new funnels and angles with you. Back on June 7 I asked you to send over some directions, even loose ones, so we could shape them into real angles and headlines together. Nadja already had a strong set going, the 78/22 angles and the second thesis about feet being the foundation, so I'd pick that thread back up. Each new funnel is aiming at a different pocket of buyers in a parade that's always moving, and the honest odds on any one idea becoming a breakout are maybe 20%, but when one lands it can carry the whole thing.

The second, and the one I'd lean on hardest, is the unit economics. It isn't an advertising problem in the usual sense, but it's the problem that makes the advertising work. Get the margin right and a good ad finally has room to pay for the next customer. That's the piece with the 90% on it, and it's what actually moves you toward the €180k.
